schools.summary: Gill pictures the friends' profound silence — concluding Job obstinate, or convicted he was right, or surprised at his knowledge — so that Job alone 'took up his parable.'
Henry weighs 'mashal,' the weighty authoritative word heading Solomon's proverbs, from a root 'to rule'; Job backs his defence with a solemn oath, an oath being an end of strife (Heb. 6:16).
Clarke: 'meshalo,' an authoritative discourse in which Job assumes great boldness and treats his friends with little ceremony; Wesley: his grave and weighty discourse.
Ellicott maps the whole remaining speech, now first called a parable — the refusal to renounce his righteousness, the fate of the wicked, and the hymn to wisdom.
Gregory the Great reads the word mystically: Holy Writ mixes the mystical into the historical, obscurities pricking the reader to a deeper sense beneath the plain.

outliers.note: Reads the naming of Job's words as a 'parable' as an invitation to a mystical sense hidden beneath the historical relation, rather than a comment on the argument itself.

schools.summary: Gill treats it as a lawful, solemn oath by the living God, in opposition to lifeless idols, made only in weighty cases to end a strife settled no other way than by appeal to God.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'deprived me of my right,' the mashal introduced like Balaam's oracles (Num. 23:7); Ellicott hears faith seeing the suffering laid on him for veiled divine purposes.
Clarke condemns 'a great want of reverence,' an irritation that cannot be justified; Wesley reads it softly — God knows his integrity yet does not plead his cause against his friends.
Henry grants Job speaks 'hardly and unbecomingly' of God, a word for which Elihu reproves him (ch. 34:5).

debates.question: Is 'who hath taken away my judgment' an irreverent complaint or the language of faith?

sides.position: an irreverent, unbecoming word, to be reproved
the confession of a faith submitting to a providence it cannot read

schools.summary: Gill: so long as breath remains, the oath of God lies upon him — a vow bound for life.
Keil and Delitzsch read the line as the parenthetical ground of the oath, 'the breath of Eloah in my nostrils' — Job swearing by the life still in him.
Clarke hears an echo of Adam's creation (Gen. 2:7): nishmathi as understanding, ruach Eloah the principle of life — a periphrasis for 'as long as I live.'
Henry: resolutions against sin should be for life; the breath, God's own gift, must not be spent breathing out wickedness but praise.

themes: while my breath is in me
the spirit of God in the nostrils

schools.summary: Gill: the wickedness forsworn includes a lie against himself — he will not speak wickedly of his own soul by confessing the hypocrisy his friends demand.
Keil and Delitzsch: not a fresh vow ('my lips shall never speak') but the attestation of a settled confession agreeing with the abiding fact.
Clarke: as he has lived in all good conscience before God, so he will continue — the oath binding tomorrow to every yesterday.
Henry: a resolution against all lying in both directions — no false confession of guilt, no false denial of truth; we may not bear false witness even against ourselves.

themes: my lips shall not speak wickedness

schools.summary: Gill: Job cannot justify the friends' doctrine — that the wicked are always punished here and men known by outward estate — for to do so would be to call evil good, a profanation.
Clarke: 'far be it' — he will not admit their harsh judgment by confessing guilt; 'your judgment is pronounced at your own risk.'
Ellicott: to admit their charge is to justify them, which he refuses; Keil and Delitzsch fix 'chalilah li' as a word of direction — Job swears not to put away his tummah/innocence.
Henry reads the explication of the oath: preparing for death, Job will not part with his religion though he lost all, nor curse God as his wife had urged (ch. 2:9).

themes: God forbid that I should justify you
till I die I will not remove my integrity

schools.summary: Gill: the righteousness held fast is not his justifying righteousness (which he'd renounce, Phil. 3:9) but the righteousness of his cause — that he wronged no man.
Clarke: a resolve to live so his conscience is void of offence (1 John 3:21); Wesley: his heart shall not reproach him with betraying his own cause and innocency.
Ellicott reads a present, 'my heart doth not reproach me for any of my days'; Keil and Delitzsch take it partitively, the heart the seat of self-knowledge.

themes: the righteousness of the cause not of works
the heart that does not reproach

schools.summary: Gill: the wish measures Job's abhorrence — he would not be in the wicked man's condition for all the world, and the enemies of the godly are wicked already.
Henry hears a proverbial form (Dan. 4:19): the portion of the wicked worse than beggar, outlaw, or galley-slave, for all their pomp.
Clarke reads it forensically — 'let my accuser be proved a lying and perjured man'; Wesley: the worst he could wish an enemy is to be a wicked man.
Ellicott: Job admits the wicked is often prosperous but has no envy of him, wishing only his adversaries to share that lot.

debates.question: What does 'let mine enemy be as the wicked' express?

sides.position: that wickedness itself is the worst of fates — the utmost he could wish an enemy
a demand that his false accuser be exposed as the guilty and perjured man

themes: let mine enemy be as the wicked
abhorrence of the wicked man's portion
no envy of the prosperous wicked

schools.summary: Clarke: 'hypocrite' mistranslates chaneph, a polluted rogue enriched by fraud, whose gain cannot ransom his soul (Matt. 16:26); Wesley: though they prosper, God takes the soul to be tried.
Gill keeps the hypocrite in religion, seeming what he is not; his hope rests on outward substance, not on Christ, and fails at death.
Ellicott: 'the hope of the godless, though he get him gain, when God taketh away his soul.'
Henry: the hypocrite deceived and undeceived; God takes away his soul (Luke 12:20), and his hope proves vanity and a lie.

debates.question: Who is the 'hypocrite' whose hope fails?

sides.position: chaneph — a polluted, dishonest rogue enriched by fraud, not a religious pretender (a mistranslation)
the hypocrite in religion, who seems what he is not

themes: gain that cannot ransom the soul

schools.summary: Gill: God hears not sinners who regard iniquity (Ps. 66:18); the wicked cry at death like the foolish virgins, but God laughs at their calamity (Prov. 1:26) — yet hears his own people.
Keil and Delitzsch set the verse in a chain of rhetorical questions whose force is that the hypocrite has neither will nor ground to pray.
Henry: true repentance is heard (Isa. 1:18), but the finally impenitent, crying earnestly under trouble, meets a heaven deaf to him (Matt. 25:11).

themes: the unheard prayer of the impenitent
trouble that drives to prayer too late

schools.summary: Gill: the hypocrite does not truly delight in God's omnipotence, omniscience, holiness, word, or people, however fair a show he makes.
Ellicott sets the godly man's 'Whom have I in heaven but thee' (Ps. 73:25) over against the hypocrite, who has no promise to plead and no assured access.
Henry: delight in God is the mark of sincerity and perseverance the hypocrite lacks; the reason he does not persevere is that he has no pleasure in it.

themes: will he delight himself in the Almighty?
delight as the mark of sincerity

schools.summary: Gill renders 'concerning the hand of God' (Broughton) — the mysterious works of providence with the wicked; Job, a teacher in prosperity (ch. 4:3), is fit to teach still.
Clarke reads 'by the hand of God' as relying on divine assistance, teaching the mind of the Almighty and concealing nothing (Chaldee: 'by the prophecy of God').
Ellicott holds both senses: 'I will teach you of the hand of God,' or 'what is in the power of God.'
Henry: Job agrees the wicked are miserable but differs on timing — judgment is deferred yet sure, 'reprieves are no pardons'; he teaches by God's strong hand (Isa. 8:11).

debates.question: Does 'by the hand of God' name the help by which Job teaches or the subject he teaches?

sides.position: the divine assistance and strength by which he teaches
the theme itself — the hand and power of God in providence

themes: I will teach you by the hand of God

schools.summary: Gill: they have seen the wicked spread like a green bay tree (Ps. 37:35) and good men afflicted, Job himself before their eyes.

Keil and Delitzsch call the verse the key to what follows — Job grants the rule (with exceptions) but denies its application to him, 'vain in vanity' (cf. Rom. 1:21); Ellicott alone refers 'ye have seen it' to Job's proclaiming God's power.
Clarke: 'why should ye babble babblings,' 'vanitize vanity'; Wesley: confirmed by their own experience, their vanity being to condemn him because afflicted.

outliers.note: Refers 'ye yourselves have seen it' not to the fate of the wicked but to Job's own proclaiming of God's power.

schools.summary: Ellicott records and rejects the theory that vv.13-23 are a lost speech of Zophar (Job deliberately echoes Zophar's conclusion, ch. 20:29), holding that Job accepts the friends' facts but not their inference; Keil and Delitzsch render the verse the title of the doom.
Gill: the portion is chiefly after death — banishment, the second death, a portion with hypocrites (Matt. 24:51) — not merely in this life.
Clarke: God sometimes shows the wicked man's doom visibly, sometimes reserves judgment for another world.

debates.question: Are vv.13-23 Job's own words or a misplaced third speech of Zophar?

sides.position: Job's own teaching, accepting the friends' facts but refusing their inference (he echoes Zophar's conclusion deliberately)
the missing third speech of Zophar, the rubric having dropped from the text

debates.question: When does the wicked man's 'portion' fall?

sides.position: chiefly after death — banishment, the second death, a portion with hypocrites
sometimes visibly in this life, sometimes reserved for the world to come

themes: the portion of a wicked man with God
Job's words or Zophar's lost speech
the facts granted, the inference refused

schools.summary: Gill: many children is an external good common to good and bad (Haman's ten sons, Ahab's seventy), no sure sign of favour.
Clarke: a large family was thought a benediction, but the wicked man's offspring are cut off by violent death or reduced to poverty.
Keil and Delitzsch: the more children he leaves, the fairer the marks for God's arrows — 'if his children multiply, it is for the sword.'
Henry ranges the three sore judgments (2 Sam. 24:13) against the seed — sword (war, justice, or murderer, cf. Esau, Gen. 27:40), famine, and pestilence.

themes: the fuller quiver the fuller sorrow
a numerous house no proof of favour

schools.summary: Gill: 'those that remain' are those left after his death, or who escaped the sword and famine, now overtaken by a further stroke.

Clarke: 'buried in death,' utter destruction with no redemption; the widows do not weep, for when the wicked perish there is shouting (Prov. 11:10); Wesley: widows plural by polygamy, tearless from relief at a tyrant's fall.

Keil and Delitzsch: the widows keep no mourning rites (cf. Gen. 23:2; Ps. 78:64), the stroke-on-stroke punishment preventing the customs and stifling pity; Ellicott: an obscure death exciting no sympathy, 'widows' either hired mourners or the widows of the survivors.

debates.question: Why do the wicked man's widows not weep?

sides.position: from relief — glad to be rid of a tyrant under whom they groaned
from a grief too stunned by successive strokes to keep the forms of mourning

themes: the widows that do not weep

schools.summary: Gill: heaping silver like dust shows the covetous bias of the mind that cannot be content, and his diligence and success.
Clarke: unsanctified wealth a curse, money the most dangerous possession, doubly cursing or blessing; Wesley: 'as clay' means in great abundance.
Keil and Delitzsch: dust and street-dirt (Zech. 9:3) are the emblem of an abundance so great it cheapens even the precious.
Henry: the worldling lades himself with thick clay (Hab. 2:6), heaping till the silver cankers and garments moth (Jas. 5:2); death will strip him.
Gill: the verse begins with the raiment mentioned last, an eastern idiom; the wicked prepares but does not enjoy.
Clarke: money is God's own (Hag. 2:8); abused for a time, God restores it to its proper use, the righteous inheriting the wicked.
Henry: the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just (Prov. 13:22; Eccl. 2:26); the innocent divides it to the poor (Prov. 28:8) — money like manure, good only if spread.

themes: the just shall wear his raiment
the wealth of the sinner laid up for the just
the sweetest irony of the portion

schools.summary: Gill: the moth builds in a garment by destroying it and is soon shaken out; the palace built with unrighteous mammon soon falls; the figure fits the hypocrite's hope.
Clarke: the moth's frail larval case, and the watchman's flimsy vineyard-booth left to the winter rains; Wesley: the moth quickly dispossessed, the booth as quickly pulled down.
Keil and Delitzsch: the palace as brittle as a moth's fine spinning — 'a hut that a watchman setteth up.'
Henry: the man secure as a moth, with no apprehension of danger, his place soon to know him no more.

debates.question: To what does the moth-image liken the wicked man's house?

sides.position: the fragile tunnel the moth eats in a garment, out of which it is shaken
the temporary case the moth spins in its larval state

themes: a house built as a moth
built for permanence, fashioned for ruin

schools.summary: Gill: either he cannot be gathered to rest for fear of losing his wealth, or his wealth 'is not gathered' (yet) and is suddenly gone.

Clarke: denied burial and a place with the righteous, opening his eyes at the resurrection to find he 'is not'; or stripped by night-marauders like Job; Wesley: lie down in death, no honourable interment, gone in the twinkling of an eye.
Ellicott: the 'gathering' of his wealth ('it is not'), or he is cut off the moment he opens his eyes; Keil and Delitzsch: 'he lieth down rich and doeth it not again.'
Henry: he bids his soul take its ease, yet his mind is never composed to enjoy, full of tossings till dawn, then he and his all hasten away.

debates.question: What does 'he shall not be gathered... he openeth his eyes, and he is not' mean?

sides.position: he is denied burial and a place with the righteous, and perishes utterly
his wealth is suddenly gone — 'he openeth his eyes, and it is not'
his mind is never gathered or composed to enjoy his abundance

themes: the rich man lies down but is not gathered
denied burial or robbed of goods

schools.summary: Gill: the terrors of death and of the guilty soul after death — conscience, the law's curses, God's wrath — coming as a flood, a Magor-missabib (Jer. 20:3).
Clarke: an irresistible flood, a tempest in the night hiding his danger; Wesley: God's wrath like a tempest, unexpected as a thief in the night.
Keil and Delitzsch: 'terrors take hold of him as a flood; by night a tempest stealeth him away' — the whirlwind of judgment over his false security.
Henry: the two despairs, silent-sullen or open-clamorous; death an east wind to the wicked, a fair gale to the godly.

themes: death — east wind or fair gale

schools.summary: Gill: the strong east wind, death armed with God's wrath; the Septuagint and Vulgate 'a burning wind' that kills at once.
Keil and Delitzsch give the qadim of the Arabian desert its natural history — the parching, devastating wind that scorches the harvest and sickens man and beast.
Clarke: the 'levanter,' the euroclydon of Acts 27:14; Wesley: a terrible judgment carrying him from the palace he thought eternal.

themes: the east wind carries him away
the wind that withers and sweeps off

schools.summary: Gill: God casts sins, wrath, and punishment on him without mercy — the God who spared not the angels, the old world, or Sodom (2 Pet. 2:4).
Clarke keeps the storm as subject, incessantly pelting him beyond escape; Wesley: God casting his plagues one after another, the man fleeing in vain.
Ellicott: the subject may be the wronged man now avenging himself, not God (though the AV supplies God); Keil and Delitzsch keep God as subject, 'before his hand he fleeth utterly away.'
Henry: the day of sparing mercy over; what God casts down (Josh. 10:11; the talent of lead, Zech. 5:7) cannot be fled.

debates.question: Who is the subject that 'casteth upon him, and spareth not'?

sides.position: God, casting his wrath without mercy
the storm or tempest, personified, which none can escape
the man he had oppressed, now avenging himself

themes: God casteth upon him and spares not
no sparing mercy in the end

schools.summary: Gill: righteous men — and, impersonally, angels and saints — clap in triumph at the display of divine justice ('hands shall be clapped at him').
Wesley: men clap in joy at the removal of a public pest, and in scorn; Clarke: the storm personified claps and hisses him off the stage, the word 'men' to be dropped as 'God' was.

debates.question: Whose hands clap and hiss the wicked man from his place?

sides.position: righteous men and applauding angels, rejoicing in God's justice
the storm of judgment personified, driving him off (the word 'men' to be omitted)

themes: men clap their hands at him
the derision of the righteous or of the storm
